# How I work

## What I'm like to work with
- I'm passionate about tech, and I want to try every new thing and build new products.
- I help others as much as I can, and I try to be available and eager to help.
- I don't watch the clock. I'll go the extra mile when it matters.
- I care about keeping our tech as debt-free as possible, and I always push for that.
- When a new technology comes out, I'm keen to dive in, try it, and report back on what we could do with it.

## How I solve problems
I don't think of an entire spec at once. I'm much better at solving problems when I'm given one. So I like to work through problems one at a time, come up with my own solutions, and then build them. I'd rather get the potential problems out before I start, instead of building from assumptions and then being told to change the whole thing.

## What people get wrong about me at first
- That I won't help them with something. I will.
- That I just agree with whoever's in charge and have no opinions of my own about tech. I do have opinions.
- That I only understand frontend. I've worked across frontend and backend.
- That I don't want to learn because I hold opinions. I do want to learn. I just want to learn it from someone who can prove me wrong.

## Hard parts I've handled
- Pressure to ship fast with AI while guardrails and testing lag behind.
- Leading one person while still delivering my own work.

# What I like building

## The thing underneath
I love solving problems, making small decisions, and improving a part of an application. Each one is a puzzle that needs me to think out of the box.

## Syraa: use what the framework already gives me
Syraa is my take on an agent harness. It doesn't have to be a coding harness. It's a harness that handles memory, context and tools, so that anyone with little knowledge of AI can use it.

I started out with a lot of custom-built stuff and quickly realised the framework has to be used with its own primitives. Standards in AI are changing quickly, and to build a harness that can keep extending as AI keeps changing, it needs to use the standard way of doing things. So I changed my mind: I began by building my own and moved to the standard way.

I use the framework's own streaming, tools, memory and storage. I keep my own domain packages for memory, context and ingestion free of framework imports, and wire them in through tools, processors and instructions. I write custom code only when nothing in the framework fits, when it's genuinely product logic, or when there's a documented workaround.

## ai-mcp-brain: tools that work with agents
I chose an agent-first install: the user pastes a one-liner pointing at an INSTALL.md, and their agent does the setup, with no shell installer. Every operating system is different, and every machine sets things up differently. I wanted the app to be able to set itself up the way each user wants. Everything is so customizable nowadays that it intrigued me. If an agent is going to use the tool, it makes sense for an AI agent to set it up too.

I also built a brainstormer skill that interviews me about an idea before any building starts. I was very much into one-shotting ideas, but I wanted the agent to take a predictable route, with the major decisions made before implementation starts. It saves output tokens, because expectations are set from the beginning. And because I solve problems best when they're put to me one at a time, the skill keeps asking me problems to solve. I come up with the solutions, and the agent implements them later. It surfaces its potential problems up front, instead of building from its own assumptions and then being told to change everything.

## A self-hosted agent for pull requests (a private project)
I designed it to run on a customer's own server. Security came first. Pull requests from forks are never allowed, because I didn't want anybody misusing the tool by creating a lot of them. Outbound network access is allowlisted, and unknown destinations wait for a human to approve, so the infrastructure is protected from malicious websites. That matters because agents get browser access so people can run end-to-end tests. I give a capability like a browser, but only with guardrails around it. I keep the details of this one vague because the project is private.

# Who I am

## The short version
I'm a normal guy who's nerdy about computer stuff, music, and learning how everything in technology works. I get paid to build software for companies, and I studied it in college. I love making software, and I like coming up with solutions to problems that can be solved with tech.

## How I got into software
My school taught Java from the 8th standard. As soon as I learnt it, I was hooked and wanted to build applications with it. I picked up a little JFrame and was amazed that I could make buttons and windows.

I played a lot of games, so next I wanted to build them. As I learnt more programming I started thinking about how games were made, and that led me to Unity and C#, because C# felt syntactically close to Java.

From there I somehow ended up in React and frontend websites, then backend APIs. Then I just fell in love with it.

## The last two years
I learnt a lot about how a growing startup works. I loved the speed, and the sheer amount of things I had to understand and implement. The last year in particular, following the AI boom and making it work inside our product, has been great: new standards, new workflows, new environments, and the speed they unlock. I've loved the process of learning, and being able to work directly on AI in our company.

The hard part is the flip side of the boom: unrealistic expectations, and everybody banking heavily on AI and expecting me to as well. If implementation is no longer the bottleneck, testing should be, and pushing code without enough guardrails and checks has been daunting.

I also took on extra responsibility as a team lead with one person under me. Training them and getting work done together taught me a lot, and it pushed me to work even harder.

## Music
I've trained in Hindustani classical music as a vocalist.
